title: Hominini
wiki_lead:
The Hominini (hominins) form a taxonomic tribe of the subfamily Homininae (hominines). They comprise two extant genera: Homo (humans) and Pan (chimpanzees and bonobos), and in standard usage exclude the genus Gorilla (gorillas), which is grouped separately within the subfamily Homininae.
The term Hominini was originally introduced by Camille Arambourg (1948), who combined the categories of Hominina and Simiina pursuant to Gray's classifications (1825).

Traditionally, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans were grouped together, excluding humans, as pongids. Since Gray's classifications, evidence accumulating from genetic phylogeny confirmed that humans, chimpanzees, and gorillas are more closely related to each other than to the orangutan. The orangutans were reassigned to the family Hominidae (great apes), which already included humans; and the gorillas were grouped as a separate tribe (Gorillini) of the subfamily Homininae. Still, details of this reassignment remain contested, and of publishing since (on tribe Hominini), not every source excludes gorillas and not every source includes chimpanzees.
Humans are the only extant species in the Australopithecine branch (subtribe), which also contains many extinct close relatives of humans.

Terminology and definition

Concerning membership, when Hominini is taken to exclude Pan, Panini ("panins") may refer to the tribe containing Pan as its only genus. Or perhaps place Pan with other dryopithecine genera, making the whole tribe or subtribe of Panini or Panina together. Minority dissenting nomenclatures include Gorilla in Hominini and Pan in Homo (Goodman et al. 1998), or both Pan and Gorilla in Homo (Watson et al. 2001).
By convention, the adjectival term "hominin" (or nominalized "hominins") refers to the tribe Hominini, whereas the members of the subtribe Hominina (and thus all archaic human species) are referred to as "homininan" ("homininans"). This follows the proposal by Mann and Weiss (1996), which presents tribe Hominini as including both Pan and Homo, placed in separate subtribes. The genus Pan is referred to subtribe Panina, and genus Homo is included in the subtribe Hominina (see below).
The alternative convention uses "hominin" to exclude members of Panina: for Homo; or for human and australopithecine species. This alternative convention is referenced in e.g. Coyne (2009) and in Dunbar (2014). Potts (2010) in addition uses the name Hominini in a different sense, as excluding Pan, and uses "hominins" for this, while a separate tribe (rather than subtribe) for chimpanzees is introduced, under the name Panini. In this recent convention, contra Arambourg, the term "hominin" is applied to Homo, Australopithecus, Ardipithecus, and others that arose after the split from the line that led to chimpanzees (see cladogram below); that is, they distinguish fossil members on the human side of the split, as "hominins", from those on the chimpanzee side, as "not hominins" (or "non-hominin hominids").

grok_lead: Hominini is a taxonomic tribe in the subfamily Homininae (hominines) of the family Hominidae, encompassing the genus Homo âincluding modern humans ( Homo sapiens)âand numerous extinct genera such as Australopithecus, Paranthropus, Ardipithecus, Orrorin, and Sahelanthropus, all more closely related to humans than to chimpanzees or gorillas. The tribe is defined by shared evolutionary traits stemming from a last common ancestor with the sister tribe Panini (comprising chimpanzees, Pan troglodytes, and bonobos, Pan paniscus), with divergence estimated between 5.5 and 6.3 million years ago based on recent molecular evidence. Originating in Africa during the late Miocene to early Pliocene epochs, Hominini represents the human lineage characterized by progressive adaptations including obligate bipedalism, increased brain size, and sophisticated tool use in later species. The classification of Hominini has evolved with advances in genetics and paleontology, including 2025 complete sequencing of ape genomes that refine divergence estimates and phylogenetic ties; prior to the 1960s, the term "hominid" was restricted to humans alone, but molecular data revealed the close phylogenetic ties between humans and African apes, prompting the expansion of Hominidae to include great apes and the redefinition of Hominini to isolate the human clade. Key early members, such as Sahelanthropus tchadensis (circa 7 million years ago), exhibit bipedal adaptations evidenced by cranial features like reduced canine morphology and foramen magnum positioning, as well as postcranial remains indicating habitual upright walking. Later genera, including Australopithecus afarensis (3.9â2.9 million years ago), demonstrate more pronounced bipedalism alongside arboreal capabilities, bridging early hominin locomotion patterns. The tribe's fossil record, primarily from East and South African sites, underscores a conservative morphological strategy with ecological plasticity, allowing adaptation to diverse habitats from woodlands to savannas. Hominini's evolutionary trajectory culminates in the genus Homo, which emerged around 2.8 million years ago with species like Homo habilis showing evidence of stone tool manufacture, marking a shift toward cultural and technological complexity. Unlike Panini, Hominini species exhibit reduced sexual dimorphism over time and enhanced cognitive capacities, as inferred from endocranial casts and archaeological assemblages. Today, Homo sapiens is the sole surviving member, having dispersed globally from Africa approximately 60,000â100,000 years ago, while all other hominins went extinct by about 40,000 years ago. This tribe's history illuminates human origins, highlighting the interplay of environmental pressures, genetic drift, and selection in shaping our species.
